title: Strong metamagnetic switching and anisotropic magnetotransport in the distorted kagome magnet Tb6Ti4Al43
authors: Lipika, Sneh, Shobha Singh, Ralf Koban, Walter Schnelle, Rie Umetsu, Kaustuv Manna
abstract: We report a comprehensive investigation of the magnetic, electrical, and thermodynamic properties of single crystalline Tb6Ti4Al43, in which Tb atoms form a distorted kagome lattice embedded within a complex Ti-Al framework. Tb6Ti4Al43 exhibits pronounced magnetic anisotropy and antiferromagnetic ordering at approximately 19 K. For magnetic field applied along the c-axis, a strong metamagnetic switching is observed, accompanied by a clear asymmetric hysteresis at low temperatures, while for field applied along the ab plane, a spin-flop transition is observed. The effect of field induced magnetic states is strongly reflected in magnetotransport measurements, giving rise to pronounced anomalies in magnetoresistance and an anomalous Hall contribution. A significant intrinsic contribution to the anomalous Hall conductivity is observed, highlighting the Berry curvature effects arising from the system's momentum-space topology. Our results highlight the interplay of spin, charge, and lattice degrees of freedom in Tb6Ti4Al43 and establish this distorted kagome antiferromagnet as a promising platform for field-tunable multifunctional behaviour, including electrically readable magnetic switching, spin manipulation, and magneto-mechanical functionalities.
summary: This work comprehensively characterizes the magnetic, electrical, and thermal properties of the distorted kagome magnet Tb6Ti4Al43. Key findings include observing field-induced metamagnetic switching and quantifying a large intrinsic contribution to the anomalous Hall effect via Berry curvature. The results establish the material as a promising platform for multifunctional spintronic applications.
main_problem: The study investigates the complex interplay between spin, charge, and lattice degrees of freedom in a distorted kagome magnet to understand its field-tunable multifunctional behavior.
main_result: The material exhibits strong magnetic anisotropy, undergoing metamagnetic switching along the c-axis and showing evidence of intrinsic Berry curvature effects contributing significantly to the anomalous Hall conductivity.
method: The research employed a combination of magnetic measurements (magnetization, specific heat), electrical transport measurements (resistivity, anomalous Hall effect), and structural characterization (XRD) on single crystals.
model_or_system: The physical system is single-crystalline Tb6Ti4Al43, which features Tb atoms forming a distorted kagome lattice embedded within a Ti-Al framework, leading to complex magnetic interactions.
key_observables: Metamagnetic switching, spin-flop transition, anomalous magnetoresistance, anomalous Hall conductivity ($\sigma_{yx}$), and magnetic ordering temperature ($T_N \sim 19 	ext{ K}$).
important_parameters: Low temperatures (2 K), magnetic fields applied along different crystal axes ($H \parallel c$ vs $H \parallel ab$), and the Curie-Weiss temperature ($	heta \sim 29 	ext{ K}$).
main_assumptions: The anomalous Hall effect is attributed to intrinsic Berry curvature effects arising from the system's momentum-space topology, despite the presence of extrinsic scattering mechanisms.
figures_summary: Figures detail atomic structure and crystal orientation (Fig. 1); magnetization vs. T and H (Figs. 2, 5); specific heat measurements (Fig. 3); and the separation of anomalous Hall contributions into skew-scattering and intrinsic quadratic terms (Fig. 8).
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure of characterization (structure, magnetism, thermodynamics) followed by detailed transport measurements, culminating in the separation and analysis of the anomalous Hall effect contributions.
why_interesting: The observation of large intrinsic Berry curvature contributions to transport properties in a magnetically ordered, geometrically frustrated system like a kagome magnet is highly relevant to topological condensed matter physics, which often overlaps with AMO/quantum simulation concepts.
